svg.text: 770,000 tons of metal is buried every year, and has been since 2001
an entrant or acquirer in metals recovery
whether the feedstock exists, and where a plant would go
buried tonnage falls without new recovery capacity opening
tons of metal-bearing residue, recovered and buried
1,018k buried in 2001, 770k in 2023; the share never leaves 50-63%. The 2015 dip is
a non-filing cycle, not a shutdown.
but the leader changed, the hard way
Horsehead held 46% of recovered tonnage in 2015 and filed Chapter 11
in 2016, with 800k tons a year going into holes beside it. Feedstock
and the plants are in the wrong states
2023 tons buried, against recovery capacity in the same state
Alabama runs 515k tons of recovery and buries 21k. Arkansas buries
168k and has no plant; Michigan buries 144k and has none. Twelve
states hold any recovery capacity at all and thirteen bury more than
10k tons, and they are mostly not the same thirteen.
2023 tons of metal-bearing residue sent to disposal, by site
87% of the buried tonnage across 64 sites: a sales list of a dozen names. Most are
incinerators and landfills sending on their own ash — the customer is the treatment
So the answer on inefficiency by year is none — the rate is flat. By size, none — the largest fifth of handlers is 94% of the tonnage and behaves like
the average. By category and by state, yes, and those two are the whole finding. The apparent adoption curve in W304 was one firm's material moving
Family is form_code in W304, W319, W504, W309, W312, W505 — single-valued, cannot inflate. Recovery is the four recovery categories; buried is
landfill, incineration and deep-well. Treatment is a third fate and is in neither. managed_tons on GM and WR rows, which do not overlap.
